claims.text: Grip the bar overhand (palms down), hands about shoulder-width apart, in a straight line with the shoulders and elbows.

quotes.text: Grip a bar with an overhand (pronated) grip, hands about shoulder-width apart.
Hold the barbell about shoulder-width apart with the palms facing down and hands in a straight line with shoulders and elbows.

claims.text: Stand with the feet hip- or shoulder-width apart, knees soft, chin slightly tucked, shoulders drawn back and down.

quotes.text: Stand with your feet hip or shoulder-width apart and give your glutes and abs a gentle squeeze
Slightly tuck your chin and look forward, maintaining a soft knee bend
Keep your shoulders drawn back and down and set them in place, creating tension through your upper back

claims.text: Lift the bar toward the shoulders by bending the elbows, keeping the elbows down close to the sides.

quotes.text: Lift the bar towards the shoulders while bending at the elbows and keeping them down close to the sides of the body.
Lift the bar with control, by flexing your elbows.

claims.text: The upper arms do not travel back during the curl; they stay at the sides or move slightly forward.

quotes.text: Don’t let your upper arm travel back during the curl. Keep it at your side or move it slightly forward.

claims.text: Swinging to get the bar up means the weight is too heavy; it lowers the effect and could hurt the joints. Control both the lift and the lowering, and start light.

quotes.text: If you can’t achieve the curling motion or control the descent of the weight without swinging your arms, you’re not recruiting the muscles properly.
Relying on momentum signals that you’re lifting above your ability. Not only does this reduce the effectiveness of the exercise, but it could also hurt your joints.
Move with control through the eccentric load (lowering) and concentric phase (curling). Start light and build the weight as you get stronger.

claims.text: Keep the wrists neutral: you should be able to draw a straight line from the hands to the elbows.

quotes.text: Your wrists should remain neutral without excessive strain on the wrists.
look at your arms and ensure you can draw a straight line from your hands to your elbows.

claims.text: Elbows flaring outward is a form fault; reduce the weight and keep the upper arms still and the elbows close to the ribs.

quotes.text: If your elbows flare outward, your form needs some work. Try reducing the weight and focusing on correct movement patterns before building.
Keep your upper arms still and elbows close to your ribcage

claims.text: Stand tall and do not arch the back while curling.

quotes.text: Bend your elbows and draw the weights toward your shoulders with control. Avoid arching your back and stand tall

claims.text: An EZ bar lets the hands sit at an angle, which Tom's Guide says eases pressure on the joints compared with a straight bar.

quotes.text: The design of EZ curl bars reduces pressure on your joints by allowing you to angle your hands and grips.

claims.text: In an isokinetic max-effort elbow-flexion test (15 young men), the biceps, brachialis and brachioradialis were all very active palm-down, palm-up and neutral.

quotes.text: The biceps, brachialis and brachioradialis muscles were electromyographically very active throughout resisted elbow flexion, in all three investigated positions of forearm rotation.
Fifteen young healthy male volunteers participated in this research.

while the subjects were performing elbow flexions/extensions with as much strength as possible, forearm in neutral position, then in full pronation, then in full supination. The elbow flexion torques were isokinetically measured at 60°/sec for an arc of 120°.

claims.text: During the lifting phase, a palms-down curl gave lower biceps and brachioradialis activity and higher front-shoulder (anterior deltoid) activity than a palms-up curl, in one EMG study of bodybuilders.

quotes.text: During the ascending phase, (i) biceps brachii excitation was greater with the supinated compared to the pronated [+19(7)%, ES: 2.60]
the brachioradialis showed greater excitation with the supinated compared to the pronated [+5(4)%, ES: 1.01]
the anterior deltoid excitation was greater with the pronated and neutral handgrip compared to the supinated condition

claims.text: StrengthLog lists the biceps as the primary muscle and the forearm flexors as secondary; coaching sources say the overhand grip works the forearms and brachioradialis harder.

quotes.text: Primary muscles worked: Biceps Secondary muscles worked: Forearm Flexors
The pronated hand position works your forearms harder, targeting and strengthening the brachioradialis muscle.

claims.text: Tempo (up = lifting, down = lowering): about 1 s up and 2 s down, inside ACSM's moderate speed of 1-2 s each way; keep tension at the bottom.

quotes.text: at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)
To accomplish this, you could try to avoid letting your elbows travel backwards during the lift, and also keep tension in the muscles in the bottom position.
Slowly lower the weights down to the starting position and repeat for reps.

claims.text: Load progression: add 2-10% load once you can do one or two reps more than the target number.

quotes.text: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

libraryDiff.why: exercises.json has forearms and brachialis primary, biceps secondary. EMG shows the biceps stays very active with the palms down (c10), and StrengthLog lists the biceps as primary (c12), so biceps moves to primary. Forearms stay primary (c12, coaching emphasis on the brachioradialis). brachialis is text-only. Coratella 2023 (c11) found less brachioradialis activity palms-down than palms-up, so the 'forearms primary' emphasis rests on coaching sources, not EMG.
